question.knowledge_point: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form
question.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x}{3{y}^{2}} \\ 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{3}={x}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}+C}.
$$

question.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,{y}^{′}=1$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}{y}^{′} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ 2{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
2{y}^{1/2}=\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C \\ {y}^{1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{C}{2} \\ y & ={(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{C}{2})}^{2} \\ y & ={(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}+K)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\frac{C}{2}.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to an Equation Containing a Transformed Reciprocal Function
question.problem:
Consider the following trigonometric  equation:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{12})=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}
$$

The general solution of this equation can be expressed as 

$$
x=a+6\pi n,\,x=-\frac{3\pi }{4}+6\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is any integer. Which of the following could be the value of $a?$
question.worked_solution:
First, note that the given equation is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{12})=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\frac{x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{12}=-\frac{2\pi }{3}+2n\pi ,\,\frac{x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{12}=-\frac{\pi }{3}+2\pi n.
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3}=\frac{\pi }{12}-\frac{2\pi }{3}+2n\pi , & \,\frac{x}{3}=\frac{\pi }{12}-\frac{2\pi }{3}+2n\pi  \\ \frac{x}{3}=-\frac{7\pi }{12}+2n\pi , & \,\frac{x}{3}=-\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi  \\ x=-\frac{7\pi }{4}+6n\pi , & \,x=-\frac{3\pi }{4}+6n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have that $a=-\frac{7\pi }{4}.$

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}(3{x}^{3})-\int (3{x}^{3})(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =3{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D) \\  & =3{x}^{3}{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}{log}_{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}(3{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{6D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})-\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$

$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$

$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Image of a Line Given by an Equation in Slope-Intercept Form
question.problem:
Consider the line $y=4x-1$ and linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the equation of the image of the line under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that the line $y=4x-1$ passes through the points $Q(0,-1)$ and $R(1,3)$ since the coordinates of both points satisfy the equation.

To find the image of $Q$ and $R$ under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing the coordinates of the points:

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -10 \\ -2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective image points are ${Q}^{′}(3,-2)$ and ${R}^{′}(-10,6).$

Finally, we write the equation of the line that passes through ${Q}^{′}$ and ${R}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =\frac{6-(-2)}{-10-3}(x-3) \\ y+2 & =-\frac{8}{13}(x-3) \\ 13y+26 & =-8x+24 \\ 8x+13y+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=0$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
question.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{y}^{2} \\ -\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{y} & =x+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{x+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x+C},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{1+C} \\ 1+C & =1 \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=0$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x}.
$$
